Sponges and cnidarians:
Invertebrates are animals without a backbone. Sponges (phylum Porifera) are simple animals that live attached to one place. Their bodies have many pores, and water flows in through the pores and out through a large opening called the osculum. Special collar cells filter tiny food particles from the water. Sponges have no true tissues, organs, or nerves.

Cnidarians include jellyfish, sea anemones, hydras, and corals. They have radial symmetry and a body with one opening, the mouth. Their tentacles carry stinging cells called cnidocytes, which they use to catch prey and defend themselves. They have a simple nerve net. Two body forms exist: the attached polyp and the free-swimming medusa.
Worms:
Worms are soft-bodied invertebrates with bilateral symmetry. There are three main groups. Flatworms (phylum Platyhelminthes), such as planarians and tapeworms, have flat bodies and a digestive system with only one opening. Many flatworms, like tapeworms and flukes, are parasites.

Roundworms (phylum Nematoda) have thin, round, unsegmented bodies and a digestive tube with a mouth and an anus. Some, like hookworms, are parasites; many live freely in soil.

Segmented worms (phylum Annelida), such as earthworms and leeches, have bodies divided into repeating segments. They have a closed circulatory system. Earthworms loosen and enrich soil.
Mollusks:
Mollusks (phylum Mollusca) are soft-bodied animals with no backbone. Most have a body with three main parts: a muscular foot, a visceral mass holding the organs, and a mantle, a skin layer that often makes a hard shell. Many use a rough tongue-like organ, the radula, to scrape food.

There are three main classes. Gastropods, such as snails and slugs, have one shell or none and move on a broad foot. Bivalves, such as clams and mussels, have two shells joined by a hinge and filter food from water. Cephalopods, such as squid and octopuses, have tentacles, a large brain, and a closed circulatory system. Most live in water, but some snails live on land.
Arthropods:
Arthropods (phylum Arthropoda) are the largest animal group. They have a hard outer covering called an exoskeleton, a segmented body, and jointed legs. To grow, they must shed the exoskeleton in a process called molting. They have an open circulatory system.

Main classes: insects have three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen), six legs, and usually two antennae and wings. Arachnids, such as spiders and scorpions, have two body parts, eight legs, and no antennae. Crustaceans, such as crabs and shrimp, usually have two pairs of antennae and live mostly in water. Myriapods, such as centipedes and millipedes, have many legs. Many insects change form in metamorphosis.
Echinoderms:
Echinoderms (phylum Echinodermata) are marine invertebrates. The name means spiny skin. Their bodies have an internal skeleton made of hard plates, and many have spines on the surface. Adults show radial symmetry, often with five parts around a center, while larvae are bilaterally symmetrical.

They move with a water vascular system, a network of water-filled canals ending in many small tube feet. Examples are sea stars, sea urchins, sand dollars, brittle stars, sea cucumbers, and sea lilies. Echinoderms have no brain. Many can regrow lost arms, and some reproduce this way. All live in salt water, and none live in fresh water.
